section.title: The Work of the Spirit
section.sectionRationale: The Upper Room Discourse draws toward its close. Jesus prepares His disciples for persecution and, astonishingly, tells them it is to their advantage that He goes away, for then He will send the Spirit. He describes the Spirit's ministry: convicting the world and guiding the disciples into all truth while glorifying Christ. He promises that their grief will turn to unshakable joy, invites bold prayer in His name, and ends with the great assurance, in the world you will have trouble, but take courage, I have overcome the world.
section.thesis: Jesus tells His disciples that His departure is for their good, since it brings the Spirit who convicts the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment and guides them into all truth while glorifying Christ, and He promises that their present grief will turn to a joy no one can take, grounded in a Father who loves them and a Savior who has overcome the world.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the warning of persecution; the advantage of Jesus' going and the convicting, guiding work of the Spirit; grief that will turn to lasting joy and the invitation to ask in His name; and the disciples' fragile faith met by the promise that Jesus has overcome the world.

units.label: Persecution foretold
units.note: so that you will not fall away

verses.text: “I have told you these things so that you will not fall away.
They will put you out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God.
They will do these things because they have not known the Father or Me.
But I have told you these things so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you about them. I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you.

units.label: The work of the Spirit
units.note: it is for your benefit that I go away

verses.text: Now, however, I am going to Him who sent Me; yet none of you asks Me, ‘Where are You going?’
Instead, your hearts are filled with sorrow because I have told you these things.
But I tell you the truth, it is for your benefit that I am going away. Unless I go away, the {{parakletos|Advocate}} will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you.
And when He comes, He will {{elencho|convict}} the world in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment:
in regard to sin, because they do not believe in Me;
in regard to righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see Me;
and in regard to judgment, because the prince of this world has been condemned.
I still have much to tell you, but you cannot yet bear to hear it.
However, when the Spirit of {{aletheia|truth}} comes, He will guide you into all truth. For He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears, and He will declare to you what is to come.
He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you.
Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine. That is why I said that the Spirit will take from what is Mine and disclose it to you.
In a little while you will see Me no more, and then after a little while you will see Me.”

units.label: Grief will turn to joy
units.note: no one will take away your joy

verses.text: Then some of His disciples asked one another, “Why is He telling us, ‘In a little while you will not see Me, and then after a little while you will see Me’ and ‘Because I am going to the Father’?”
They kept asking, “Why is He saying, ‘a little while’? We do not understand what He is saying.”
Aware that they wanted to question Him, Jesus said to them, “Are you asking one another why I said, ‘In a little while you will not see Me, and then after a little while you will see Me’?
Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy.
A woman has pain in childbirth because her time has come; but when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world.
So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy.
In that day you will no longer ask Me anything. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you.
Until now you have not asked for anything in My name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.

units.label: I have overcome the world
units.note: in Me you may have peace

verses.text: I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you this way, but will tell you plainly about the Father.
In that day you will ask in My name. I am not saying that I will ask the Father on your behalf.
For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.
I came from the Father and entered the world. In turn, I will leave the world and go to the Father.”
His disciples said, “See, now You are speaking plainly and without figures of speech.
Now we understand that You know all things and that You have no need for anyone to question You. Because of this, we believe that You came from God.”
“Do you finally believe?” Jesus replied.
“Look, an hour is coming and has already come when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and you will leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.
I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have {{nikao|overcome}} the world!”

parakletos.gloss: Advocate, Comforter, Helper, Counselor, one called alongside. Jesus insists it is to the disciples' advantage that He go, because only then will He send the Advocate. The Spirit is no lesser substitute but the ongoing presence of God with and in His people, continuing and applying the work of Christ once He has returned to the Father.

elencho.gloss: To convict, expose, prove guilty, bring to conviction. The Spirit convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment, exposing the world's guilt in rejecting Christ, vindicating His righteousness by His going to the Father, and announcing that the prince of this world is already condemned. It is the Spirit's work to press the truth of Christ home to consciences.

aletheia.gloss: Truth. The Spirit is the Spirit of truth who guides the disciples into all truth, not by speaking on His own but by declaring what He hears and disclosing what belongs to Christ. This promise undergirds the apostolic witness and Scripture, for the Spirit leads Christ's people into the full truth about Him and glorifies Him in doing so.

nikao.gloss: To overcome, conquer, be victorious. Jesus' final word before His prayer is that He has overcome the world. Though the cross lies just ahead, He speaks of victory as good as won, so that His people can face tribulation with courage, resting in a triumph already secured by the one who conquers the world and its prince.

basic.context: As His departure nears, Jesus warns the disciples plainly that they will face expulsion and even death, so that they will not be caught off guard and fall away. Then He says something startling: it is for their good that He goes away, because only then will He send the Spirit, the Advocate. He describes the Spirit's work, convicting the world about sin, righteousness, and judgment, and guiding the disciples into all truth while glorifying Christ. He promises that their sorrow, like a woman in labor, will turn to lasting joy, invites them to ask the Father in His name, and closes with courage: in the world you will have trouble, but I have overcome the world.
basic.hermeneutics: The surprising claim is that Jesus' going is a gain, not just a loss, because it brings the Spirit and a new, universal presence of God with His people. The key questions are, what does the Spirit do, and how can the disciples have joy and peace amid trouble. The Spirit convicts the world and leads believers into truth about Christ; joy comes because the grief of the cross gives way to the joy of the resurrection and the Father's love. The final word frames the whole Christian life: real trouble, but a victory already won.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter centers on the parakletos, the Advocate, whom Jesus will send. This Spirit of aletheia, truth, will guide the disciples into all truth, and will elencho, convict, the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment. And Jesus ends with nikao: take courage, I have overcome the world.
basic.typology: The image of a woman in labor whose pain turns to joy echoes prophetic pictures of Israel's travail giving way to deliverance, now fulfilled in the sorrow of the cross turning to resurrection joy. The overcoming of the world fulfills the ancient hope of God's triumph over evil.
basic.christ: Christ sends the Spirit who glorifies Him, and everything the Spirit discloses is Christ's. He is the one whose going brings the Spirit, whose death and resurrection turn grief to joy, and who has overcome the world and its prince.
basic.god: The Father loves the disciples because they love the Son and believe He came from God. He hears prayer offered in the Son's name, and He is with the Son even when all forsake Him. The Father, Son, and Spirit work together for the people of God.
basic.crossReferences: John 14 and 15 give the other Paraclete promises. Acts 2 records the Spirit's coming. 1 John 5 speaks of overcoming the world by faith. Isaiah 26 pictures the travail turning to new life.
basic.oneStory: Jesus' departure is no defeat but the doorway to the age of the Spirit, who convicts the world, leads the church into truth, and glorifies Christ. The sorrow of the cross gives way to resurrection joy that no one can take, and the whole story rests on the triumphant word: I have overcome the world.

context.literary:
John 16 is the third and last movement of the long farewell that began at John 13:31, and it is built to be heard against chapters 14 and 15. The Spirit promises of 14:16 to 17, 14:26 and 15:26 to 27 each told the disciples what the Spirit is. Here the focus turns to what the Spirit does, to the world in verses 8 to 11 and to the disciples in verses 12 to 15. The chapter then loops back to its opening worry. It begins with 'so that you will not fall away' in verse 1 and ends with 'so that in Me you may have peace' in verse 33, and in between the same phrase, 'I have told you these things,' marks each turn, verses 1, 4, 25 and 33. Jesus is steadily naming His own purpose for speaking.

The middle of the chapter is a small drama of misunderstanding. Verses 16 to 19 repeat the phrase 'a little while' until it becomes a stumbling refrain, and the disciples mutter to one another instead of asking. Jesus answers the question they would not put, verse 19, and gives the birth image of verse 21 as the key. The pattern of sorrow turning to joy then governs verses 20 to 24, and the word 'joy' closes verses 20, 22 and 24 in turn.

There is also a movement from veiled to plain speech. Verse 25 promises that the hour is coming when He will 'tell you plainly about the Father.' In verse 29 the disciples announce that He is already speaking plainly, and Jesus' quiet reply, 'Do you finally believe?', in verse 31 sets their confidence beside the scattering He then predicts. The discourse that began with a servant's towel ends with a prediction of desertion, and then, in the final line, with a victory announced in advance. John deliberately places 'in the world you will have tribulation' next to 'I have overcome the world' in the same verse, so that neither is heard alone.
context.historical:
The warning of verses 2 and 3 is the sharpest in the discourse. 'They will put you out of the synagogues' uses a word, aposynagogos, that appears in the New Testament only in John, here and in 9:22 and 12:42. It names a painful rupture. The first Jewish followers of Jesus belonged to the synagogue by birth and worship, and being expelled cost them community, livelihood and the shared life of their people. John's Gospel was written for believers who knew this loss, and the earlier mentions in chapters 9 and 12 show the pressure was already felt around Jesus Himself.

The second warning goes further. Anyone who kills you 'will think he is offering a service to God.' The word for service, latreia, is the ordinary word for sacred worship, the kind offered at the altar. Persecution would come from sincere religious people who believed they were defending God. Paul is the living example. He later said he was convinced he ought to do all he could to oppose the name of Jesus, Acts 26:9, and he voted against believers, Acts 26:10. Jesus names the root in verse 3: they will act this way 'because they have not known the Father or Me.' Zeal without knowledge of God can be lethal.

The setting is the night of the Passover meal, probably within hours of the arrest. The disciples are Galilean fishermen, a tax collector and others, still thinking of a kingdom to be restored to Israel. They have no category for a Messiah who leaves. That is why Jesus can say in verse 12 that He has more to say but they cannot yet bear it. The 'little while' of verse 16 would prove to be about three days, from the cross to the first sighting of the risen Lord, though Jesus seems to be speaking to a longer horizon as well, as the debates below explain. The scattering of verse 32, each to his own home, would happen within the night, and it fulfils a word of the prophets, Zechariah 13:7: 'Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.'
context.canonical:
The Spirit sayings of chapters 14 to 16 are the Bible's fullest explanation of what happens between Easter and the return of Christ. They look back to the promises of Ezekiel 36:26 and 27 and Joel 2:28 and 29, where God says He will put His Spirit within His people and pour Him out on all flesh. Those promises were about a new covenant condition, not a few prophets receiving an occasional visit. Jesus tells the disciples the day has come, and that His departure is the way it comes.

The New Testament shows each promise fulfilled. In Acts 2 the Spirit falls at Pentecost, and Peter's sermon exposes the crowd's guilt over the crucifixion. When they are 'cut to the heart,' Acts 2:37, they ask what to do and are told to repent and receive forgiveness. That is the convicting work of verses 8 to 11 in action: sin, because they had not believed; righteousness, because God had made this Jesus both Lord and Christ, Acts 2:36; judgment, because the ruler of this age was beaten. The leading into truth shows in the apostolic writings, which Jesus anticipated by telling the disciples that the Spirit would declare what is to come, verse 13. Paul says the Spirit searches the depths of God and teaches believers what has been freely given, 1 Corinthians 2:10 to 13. And John himself writes that believers have an anointing that teaches them, 1 John 2:20 and 27.

The woman in labor of verse 21 is an Old Testament image the disciples would have recognised. Isaiah uses it for the anguish before deliverance, Isaiah 26:17 to 19 and 66:7 to 14, and Micah for Israel's suffering until the one who bears has given birth, Micah 5:3. Paul takes the same picture for all creation groaning 'in the pains of childbirth,' Romans 8:22. Finally the last line of the chapter returns throughout the New Testament. John says that everyone born of God overcomes the world and that the victory is faith, 1 John 5:4 and 5. And the Lion of the tribe of Judah 'has triumphed,' Revelation 5:5, with the same verb Jesus uses in verse 33.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wrote to a community that was being pushed out of synagogues and worried about the delay of the Lord's return. He placed this chapter in the Gospel to answer two fears. The first is that Jesus' absence is simply loss. John wants his readers to hear Jesus Himself call it a benefit, verse 7, and to see why: the Spirit makes Christ's presence universal, internal and permanent, where His bodily presence in Galilee could only be local. The second fear is that suffering means God has failed. Jesus told His followers about the persecution beforehand, verses 1 to 4, so that when it came they would 'remember that I told you,' and take the opposition as foreseen, not as a refutation. The disciples' immediate failure is given no softening. Their boasted faith in verses 29 and 30 breaks within hours, verse 32, and John records it so that readers will see the peace of verse 33 does not depend on the strength of their grip.

The chapter also guards a view of the Spirit. He does not speak 'on His own,' verse 13, and He does not draw attention to Himself. His work is to take from what is Christ's and disclose it, verse 14. John wanted believers to test claims about the Spirit by this standard: where the Spirit is truly present, Christ is magnified, and the Father's gifts to the Son are made known. And he wanted the readers to take heart. The final sentence is not a platitude. It is a victory announced by the one who was about to be arrested, and John expects it to hold when his readers are on the wrong end of a synagogue ban.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of this chapter is promise addressed to a particular group on a particular night. The 'you' of verse 13, who will be led into all truth and told what is to come, is first the eleven who had been with Jesus from the beginning, 15:27. That does not make it a general promise that every believer will receive new revelation. It makes it a promise that the apostles' witness would be complete and trustworthy, and that the church inherits that witness in the New Testament. Believers today are not promised new doctrines but the same Spirit who illumines the apostolic word, 1 Corinthians 2:12.

Description and command need separating in the other direction too. The scattering of verse 32 and the denial it leads to are described, not recommended. The disciples' sorrow in verse 20 is real and Jesus does not rebuke it. He says they will weep, and He promises the joy. What carries over as instruction is the pattern: expect opposition, do not take it as a sign that you have been abandoned, ask the Father in Jesus' name, verses 23 and 24, and take courage, verse 33. The promise that 'whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you' is real but sits inside the relationship the chapter describes. To ask in His name is to ask as one who belongs to Him, in line with His revealed purpose, and it should not be read as a blank cheque on our own plans.

debates.question: What does the Spirit's conviction of the world mean?

views.label: Conviction that leads to repentance
views.case: The Spirit exposes sin, righteousness and judgment so that people see their need and turn to Christ. The pattern of Acts 2:37 to 38 fits: the crowd is cut to the heart and repents. On this reading the three items are the content of gospel preaching. Sin is unbelief in Christ, righteousness is His vindication by going to the Father, judgment is the defeat of the prince of this world.

views.label: Conviction that exposes and condemns
views.case: The Greek verb elencho can mean to expose or prove wrong, as at John 3:20. On this view the Spirit's work with the world is a legal showing that the world is guilty, which may or may not end in repentance. The word 'world' in John is usually hostile, and verse 3 says they do not know the Father. Those who refuse the exposure stand condemned, verse 11.

views.label: Both, depending on the response
views.case: Many interpreters hold that the Spirit's single act of exposure has two possible outcomes. Where it is received, it leads to repentance and faith; where it is refused, it hardens into the condemnation Jesus speaks of in 3:18 to 19. This fits the way John uses light elsewhere, as the same light that saves some and exposes others.

debates.bearing: Whichever view is taken, the Spirit's work is tied to the testimony about Jesus, and he works through the witness of the disciples, 15:26 to 27. The practical bearing is that believers do not need to produce conviction themselves. Their task is to bear faithful witness; making the world see its guilt is the Spirit's task.

debates.question: What is the 'little while' of verse 16?

views.label: The three days from cross to resurrection
views.case: The immediate context fits. Within hours Jesus will be taken, and after a short time He will be seen alive. The weeping and rejoicing of verse 20 match the disciples' grief on Friday and their joy on Easter evening, 20:20, when John says the disciples 'rejoiced' at seeing the Lord.

views.label: The period between the ascension and the return
views.case: The 'little while' is the whole age of the church. Jesus leaves, the world rejoices over His absence, and the disciples grieve until He returns, when no one will take away their joy. The woman in labor then pictures the world's last pains before the new age, as in Romans 8:22 and Isaiah 26:17 to 19.

views.label: A layered fulfillment
views.case: Others hold that Jesus speaks at two levels. The resurrection is the first seeing, and the final return is the last, with the Spirit's coming at Pentecost as a bridge that makes Christ present between them. Verse 22, 'I will see you again,' leaves room for all of this.

debates.bearing: John tells us the disciples did not understand, verse 18, so the first hearers heard it only partly. The text does not make us choose; the resurrection joy is real and also a pledge of the joy still to come.

debates.question: Does the promise of 'all truth' belong to the apostles alone or to every believer?

views.label: The apostles only, as the foundation of the New Testament
views.case: The promise that the Spirit will bring to mind what Jesus said, 14:26, and declare what is to come, 16:13, suits the eleven who had been with Him from the beginning. Their Spirit led witness became the New Testament, and the church is built on that foundation, Ephesians 2:20.

views.label: Every believer receives the Spirit's teaching
views.case: John's own letter says that believers have an anointing from the Holy One and 'all of you know,' and that the anointing teaches them, 1 John 2:20 and 27. On this view the same Spirit leads all believers into the truth of Christ, though not into new revelation.

views.label: A primary application to the apostles and a derived one to all
views.case: The promise was first made to the eleven, and the New Testament is its result. The church then receives that completed witness and is taught by the same Spirit to understand and obey it.

debates.bearing: On every view the Spirit does not speak independently of Christ, verses 13 and 14. Any claimed new teaching is tested by whether it agrees with and honors what Christ has already given.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb that carries the Spirit's whole mission to the world, elencho, in verse 8. It does not mean to scold or merely to make someone feel bad. In John it is the word for exposing something so that it is seen for what it is, as in 3:20, where evildoers hate the light lest their deeds be exposed. In 8:46 Jesus asks which of His opponents can convict Him of sin, meaning prove it. In Matthew 18:15 the same verb is used of showing a brother his fault. The idea is a demonstration that carries a verdict. That is why the three objects of verses 9 to 11 are each given a 'because' clause: sin because they do not believe, righteousness because I go to the Father, judgment because the ruler of this world has been condemned. The tense of that last verb is the perfect passive, kekritai, and it presents the condemnation as an accomplished fact whose result stands. Satan's judgment is settled at the cross, which Jesus described in 12:31 as the moment the ruler of this world would be cast out.

The guiding of verse 13 is hodegeo, built on hodos, the road. The Spirit is the guide who leads along the way. Jesus has already called Himself 'the way, the truth and the life' in 14:6, so the Spirit does not guide away from Christ but further along Him. The same verb is used in Acts 8:31, where the Ethiopian says he cannot understand the prophet without someone to guide him. In verses 13 to 15 the verb for what the Spirit does with what he hears is anangello, which appears three times: 'declare' in verse 13 and 'disclose' in verses 14 and 15. The repetition shows a chain of transmission: the Father gives to the Son, the Son's things are announced by the Spirit to the disciples, and the disciples pass them on. Nothing is invented at any link.

The Greek of verse 21 is a precise picture. The woman has 'pain,' lype, in verse 21, but the child is born and she forgets her 'anguish,' thlipsis. The word thlipsis returns in verse 33 as the 'tribulation' the disciples will have in the world. Jesus uses the same word for the labour and for their persecution, which invites the reader to hear their trouble as the pains of a birth and not as a dead end. It also explains why 'tribulation' was one of the standard words in the early church for the suffering of the last days, as in Romans 8:35 and Revelation 7:14.

The verb 'ask' shifts in verses 23 and 26. In verse 23 the disciples will no longer 'ask' Jesus questions, using the verb erotao that they have just used among themselves in the dispute over the little while, and then they will 'ask' the Father, aiteo, in His name. In verse 26 the same pairing appears. John uses both verbs for requesting elsewhere, and scholars do not agree on how sharp the difference is, so it is safest to say simply that Jesus moves them from asking Him for explanations to asking the Father directly. The name is the key. In Hebrew thought a name stood for a person's character and authority, so to ask in Jesus' name is to ask on the basis of who He is and what He has done.

Last, the word for overcome in verse 33 is nikao, in the perfect tense, nenikeka: 'I have overcome.' It is a victory with lasting effect, announced while the arrest is hours away. The noun nike is the one John uses in 1 John 5:4 for the believer's faith as the victory that has overcome the world. The Greek also keeps the word for peace, eirene, tied to 'in Me.' Peace is located in a person and not in circumstances, because the circumstances, 'tribulation' in the world, are promised to stay hard.

typology.fulfillment: Israel's prophets used childbirth for the suffering that comes before deliverance, Isaiah 26:17 to 19, Isaiah 66:7 to 14 and Micah 5:3. Isaiah 26 even ends in resurrection: 'Your dead will live.' Jesus draws on this tradition to explain His own death. The sorrow of Friday is the labor; the joy of Easter is the birth, and what is born is the new age and the new people. The escalation is that the birth is not a recovery of Israel's fortunes but the beginning of new creation, which Paul later says is still groaning toward its full delivery, Romans 8:22. The picture also falls short in one respect. A mother's pain ends with her child's arrival, but Jesus Himself is both the one who suffers and the firstborn from the dead, Colossians 1:18.

typology.type: The scattering of the sheep, John 16:32
typology.fulfillment: Zechariah 13:7 describes a shepherd struck by the sword and a flock scattered, and Jesus applies it to the night of His arrest, as Matthew 26:31 and Mark 14:27 record. John 10 had already presented Jesus as the shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, and now the picture is darkly complete. The pattern is of a leader's death leaving his people vulnerable. In Christ the pattern escalates: the shepherd is raised, and gathers the scattered flock again. The scattered disciples are found on the shore in John 21. The type falls short only in that the first shepherds in Israel failed their sheep, Ezekiel 34, while this Shepherd is not lost to them.

typology.type: Joy that no one takes away, John 16:22
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament knew the promise that God would turn mourning to joy, Jeremiah 31:13, and that weeping may last for a night but joy comes with the morning, Psalm 30:5. Jesus claims that promise for His disciples and ties its fulfillment to seeing Him alive. The correspondence is between a dark night and a morning. The escalation is that the morning is permanent, since 'no one will take away your joy.' The psalm's joy came after a particular distress and could be lost again in the next one; the joy of the risen Christ rests on a victory that cannot be reversed, and the Spirit sustains it in tribulation, as Paul says in 1 Thessalonians 1:6.

study.christ:
The chapter presents Christ as the one whose departure is more useful than His presence, and that is a remarkable thing for any person to claim. He can say it because His going is the cross, resurrection and ascension, and the Spirit's coming depends on that sequence. In the earlier chapters He had said the Spirit would be sent in His name, 14:26, and from the Father, 15:26. Here He says 'I will send Him,' verse 7. The Spirit is therefore the Spirit of the Father and the Son, and Christ stands in the position of giving what only God can give. John 7:39 had already explained that the Spirit was not yet given because Jesus was not yet glorified. The sequence is fixed: Christ's glorification comes first, and the Spirit's coming follows.

The Spirit's work in turn is entirely about Christ. He convicts about unbelief in Christ, verse 9, about Christ's return to the Father, verse 10, and about the defeat of Christ's enemy, verse 11. He glorifies Christ, verse 14, by taking what is Christ's and making it known. And verse 15 gives an extraordinary reason: 'Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine.' That claim covers everything the Father has, which is the language of full divine sharing, and it explains why the Spirit's disclosure of Christ's things is also a disclosure of the Father's. In 17:10 He says the same to the Father: 'All I have is Yours, and all You have is Mine.'

Christ also appears as the one who knows what the disciples cannot yet say. In verse 19 He reads their unspoken question and answers it. In verse 30 the disciples say that He knows all things and needs no one to question Him, and Jesus does not correct the claim, though He corrects their confidence about themselves. His foreknowledge extends to their desertion, verse 32, and is no reason for Him to withdraw. He stays the whole night and prays for them in chapter 17.

Finally, Christ is the victor. 'I have overcome the world' is said before the arrest, because the cross is not the loss of the battle but its decisive engagement. Paul will say that on the cross He disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them, Colossians 2:15. Hebrews says He shared our flesh and blood to destroy the one who holds the power of death, Hebrews 2:14. The danger in reading this chapter is to treat the victory as an escape from tribulation; Jesus does not. He is the one who has gone through the trouble and come out, and His people follow Him through it, not around it. The Spirit makes that following possible, because the same Spirit who raised Christ now dwells in them, Romans 8:11.
study.god:
The first thing the chapter shows about God is that He is Trinitarian in action without ever being abstract. The Father sends the Son, verses 5, 27 and 28; the Son sends the Spirit, verse 7; the Spirit speaks what He hears and glorifies the Son, verses 13 and 14; and the Son says everything the Father has is His, verse 15. These verses were central in the early church's reasoning toward the doctrine of the Trinity, not because they give a formula but because they show three persons who are distinct in role and united in what they share. The Spirit is not an impersonal force. He 'hears,' 'speaks,' 'declares' and 'takes,' and Jesus calls Him 'He' even though the Greek word for spirit is neuter, a grammatical point that John does not smooth over.

The chapter also shows a God who is open about the price. He does not lure the disciples with ease. The warning in verses 1 to 4 is a form of love, since a Father who knew the cost and said nothing would be less than good. And He is not distant in the cost. Verse 27 says the Father Himself loves the disciples, which is startling given what Jesus has just said about their coming desertion. The ground for the love is not the strength of their commitment but their relationship with the Son: 'because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God.' The Father's love is stable where theirs is not.

God's sovereignty and human weakness sit side by side. Jesus predicts the scattering in verse 32 as something that will happen, and also says the Father is with Him in it. The Son is not rescued from loneliness by escaping it, but because the Father does not leave. That affirms both the real abandonment of men and the unbroken fellowship within God. It also shows that what the disciples fear, being left alone, is what Jesus bears for them.

Finally, the chapter shapes worship and prayer. A God who invites His people to ask in the Son's name, verses 23 and 24, is a God who delights to give, so that joy may be 'complete,' verse 24. Prayer is not a technique for getting God's attention; Jesus says plainly in verse 26 that He is not saying He will ask the Father on their behalf in the way they might fear, because the Father Himself loves them. Prayer is therefore a child speaking to a loving Father with the Son's authority. And praise follows from the final verse. If God has already overcome the world, then worship is the right response before the evidence is in. Believers can sing in tribulation, as Paul and Silas did in prison, Acts 16:25, because the outcome has been announced by the one who holds it.

crossReferences.note: The first Paraclete promise. The Father will give 'another Advocate,' the Spirit of truth, who is with the disciples and will be in them. Chapter 16 adds what He does to the world and how He relates to Christ's words. Together they show that the Spirit continues the presence of Jesus, so that He is not replaced by a lesser substitute.

The Spirit will 'teach you all things and remind you of everything I have told you.' This is the background for 16:13. Teaching and remembering mean the disciples' later writing is the Spirit's work on Jesus' own words, which is why John can write such long discourses accurately years afterward.

The Spirit will testify about Jesus, and the disciples will testify too. The Spirit's witness and the disciples' witness are joined, so that the convicting of the world in 16:8 happens through the church's proclamation. The Spirit does not work apart from the message.

The narrator's comment on the rivers of living water: the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified. It explains why Jesus' going is necessary, 16:7. His glorification at the cross and ascension opens the door to the Spirit's new coming.

The convicting work in practice. Peter tells the crowd that God has made the crucified Jesus Lord and Christ; they are 'cut to the heart' and ask what to do. Sin, righteousness and judgment appear in this one sermon, and the gift of the Spirit follows repentance.

A birth image for the end of exile: Zion labors and gives birth to a nation, and God promises comfort 'as a mother comforts her son.' Jesus' picture of the woman in labor draws on this stream, in which pain gives way to a rejoicing that is shared by those who mourned.

'Strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.' The prophecy behind the scattering of John 16:32. The disciples' flight is not a surprise to God but part of the pattern foretold, and the promise of gathering follows in the same prophecy.

John tells believers that they have an anointing from the Holy One, and in verse 27 that the anointing teaches them about all things. It shows how the Spirit's guiding into truth works for the whole church, and why John can say they know the truth without needing a new teacher.

'This is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith.' John applies Jesus' last word in 16:33 to believers, saying that those born of God overcome the world by believing that Jesus is the Son of God. The victory is Christ's and is shared by faith.

Creation groans 'in the pains of childbirth,' and believers who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan for their adoption. Paul picks up the labor image of John 16:21 and gives it its full scale. The Spirit is the pledge that the birth will be completed.

Christ 'disarmed the rulers and authorities' and triumphed over them by the cross. It reads as a commentary on 16:11 and 16:33: the ruler of this world is condemned, and the victory is won on the cross and not in spite of it.

The Lion of Judah 'has triumphed' to open the scroll. The verb is the one Jesus uses of Himself in John 16:33. The victory announced the night before the cross is celebrated in heaven's throne room, and the one who triumphs is the Lamb who was slain.

study.oneStory:
John 16 sits at the hinge between the Gospel's story of Jesus on earth and the Bible's story of the church in the world. The long thread of creation, fall and promise had always pointed to a day when God would dwell with His people, not at a distance in a tent or temple but within them. Eden was the first place of that nearness, and it was lost when Adam and Eve hid from the sound of the Lord walking in the garden, Genesis 3:8. The tabernacle and the temple gave a limited return, with God's presence enclosed behind a veil and open to one priest once a year. The prophets looked past them. Ezekiel 36:27 promised 'I will put My Spirit within you.' Joel 2:28 promised an outpouring on all people. Jeremiah 31:33 spoke of a law written on hearts. All of them expected a God who is no longer outside the camp.

This chapter says how that expectation comes about, and it is not by repairing the old structures but by a departure. Christ must go through the cross, the empty tomb and the ascension, and only then can the Spirit be sent to live in believers. The loss of Christ's visible presence is the price of a far larger gift, the indwelling of God in every believer wherever they are. That is why Jesus says the going is to their advantage.

The chapter also answers the question of how the people of God can live in a world still under the curse. The disciples are told plainly that tribulation will continue. Persecution, expulsion and death are not signs that the promise has failed, because they were the lot of the prophets and of the Son. The curse of Genesis 3 has been broken at its root, but its effects remain until the end. The labor image says this in a picture: the pain is real, the delivery is certain, and the child is the new creation, which is the people of God made alive and the world made new.

The story then runs forward. At Pentecost, Acts 2, the Spirit is poured out. In the letters He is the guarantee of the inheritance, Ephesians 1:13 to 14, and the one who makes believers cry 'Abba, Father,' Romans 8:15. In the last chapter of the Bible He joins the Bride in saying 'Come,' Revelation 22:17. The joy that no one can take away becomes visible when 'God Himself will be with them,' and He will wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:3 to 4. The scattered disciples end as a great multitude who have come out of the tribulation, Revelation 7:14. What Jesus says in the upper room as an encouragement for one anxious night is the whole shape of the church's age: the Spirit given, the world confronted, the tribulation endured, and the victory already won.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus say it is to the disciples' advantage that He goes away?

options.text: Because only if He goes will He send the Advocate, the Spirit, to be with and in them.
options.note: Verse 7 ties the sending of the Spirit to Jesus' departure.

options.text: Because they had grown tired of His presence.
options.note: The reason is the coming of the Spirit, not any weariness with Jesus.

options.text: Because they needed to carry on the mission without leaning on Him.
options.note: They are sent on mission, but the reason given is not self-reliance; it is that His going brings the indwelling Spirit.

options.text: Because His leaving would bring a new work of God among them.
options.note: True in direction, but it does not name the specific gift, the sending of the Advocate.

quiz.q: What does the Spirit do in relation to the world?

options.text: He convicts the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.
options.note: Verses 8 to 11 describe the Spirit's convicting work toward the world.

options.text: He leaves the world entirely alone.
options.note: The Spirit actively convicts the world, not ignores it.

options.text: He presses conviction that always results in repentance.
options.note: The Spirit's conviction can lead to repentance, but it also exposes and hardens; it does not compel belief in all.

options.text: He exposes the world's guilt regarding Christ.
options.note: True, but it omits the threefold scope, sin, righteousness, and judgment.

quiz.q: What does the Spirit of truth do for the disciples?

options.text: He guides them into all truth and glorifies Christ by disclosing what is His.
options.note: Verses 13 and 14 describe the Spirit guiding into truth and glorifying Christ.

options.text: He reveals new things that go beyond what Christ taught.
options.note: He does declare what is to come, but only what He hears, taking from what is Christ's; He does not speak independently of Him.

options.text: He replaces the need to know Christ at all.
options.note: The Spirit's aim is to glorify Christ, not to bypass Him.

options.text: He leads them into deeper understanding of the truth.
options.note: True, but it omits that He does so by taking what is Christ's and glorifying Him.

quiz.q: How does Jesus describe the coming change from grief to joy?

options.text: Like a woman whose labor pain turns to joy at her child's birth, their sorrow will become joy no one can take.
options.note: Verses 20 to 22 use childbirth to picture grief turning to lasting joy.

options.text: Their grief will simply be forgotten with time.
options.note: It is not mere forgetting; the sorrow itself gives way to a joy no one can take, tied to seeing Him again.

options.text: They will never feel any sorrow at all.
options.note: He acknowledges real sorrow now, which will turn to joy.

options.text: Their sorrow will give way to joy when they see Him again.
options.note: True, but it omits the vivid childbirth image and the promise that no one can take the joy.

quiz.q: What is Jesus' final word of assurance in the chapter?

options.text: In the world you will have trouble, but take courage, I have overcome the world.
options.note: Verse 33 holds together real tribulation and Christ's victory.

options.text: In the world you will have no trouble at all.
options.note: He promises trouble, but also victory over it.

options.text: Their courage will make the world's opposition fade.
options.note: They are to take courage, but not because opposition ends; their peace rests on Christ having overcome the world.

options.text: They can have peace in Him despite tribulation.
options.note: True, but it omits the ground of that peace, that He has overcome the world.

questions: Jesus called His departure an advantage because it brought the Spirit. Where are you grieving a loss that God may be using to give something greater?
The Spirit's work is to glorify Christ and disclose what is His. How can you cooperate with the Spirit's aim rather than seeking spiritual experiences detached from Jesus?
Jesus promised a joy that no one can take away. What threatens your joy, and how does the resurrection secure a joy beyond its reach?
The Father Himself loves you, Jesus said, because you love and believe in the Son. How does it steady you to know the Father's own love rests on you?
In the world you will have trouble, but I have overcome the world. How does Christ's victory change the way you face your current tribulation?

translationNotes.note: Advocate renders parakletos; the BSB footnote gives Comforter, Helper, or Counselor. Jesus insists His going secures the Spirit's coming.

In a little while you will see Me again; the BSB footnote notes some manuscripts add because I go away to the Father. The saying points to the brief separation of the cross and the joy of the resurrection.
The image of a woman in childbirth was a common Jewish metaphor for the birth pangs preceding messianic deliverance, here applied to grief turning to resurrection joy.
I have overcome the world uses the language of conquest; though the cross lies ahead, Jesus speaks of the victory as already secured.
